title: Why do drops form on a cold cup?
question: Where do the drops on the outside of a cold cup come from?
steps: Drag ice with your finger into the cup.
Watch for drops on the outside of the cup.
Use the button at the bottom left to pick a humid day or a dry day.
At the end, drag the air up the mountain.
observe: When ice makes the cup cold, the air around the cup gets cold too, and the water vapor in the air forms drops on the outside of the cup. On a humid day it takes only a little cold; on a dry day the cup must get much colder. Air that climbs a mountain gets cold too, and a cloud forms.

terms.name: Water vapor
terms.description: Water mixed into the air that you cannot see.

terms.name: Condensation
terms.description: When air gets cold, its water vapor turns into tiny drops of water.

terms.name: Dew
terms.description: Drops on a cold leaf or a cold cup: water vapor from the air.

terms.name: Cloud
terms.description: Tiny drops of water made when air rises high and gets cold.

law.equation: air gets cold → water vapor turns into drops (condensation)
law.title: Dew and clouds
law.description: When air gets cold, its water vapor turns into tiny drops of water (condensation). On a cold cup it makes dew; in air that rises high and gets cold it makes clouds. On a humid day, with lots of water vapor, a little cold is enough.

tip: Drag the top ice cube from the bowl with one finger and let go over the cup: it drops in. In the last stage, drag the air at the foot of the mountain up along the mountain.

predict.question: Where do the drops on the outside of a cold cup come from?

choices.label: They leaked out of the cup

predict.reason: The air around the cup got cold, so the water vapor in the air turned into drops. The water in the cup does not leak.
predict.bridge: Put some ice in and see!

stages.text: Put in ice and make drops form on the cup!
stages.say: On a humid day the air has lots of water vapor. The cup only has to get a little cold for drops to form.

stages.text: Make drops form on a dry day too!
stages.say: On a dry day the air has little water vapor. So the cup must get much colder for drops to form.
stages.win: Drops on a dry day too!

stages.text: Drag the air up the mountain and make a cloud!
stages.say: The higher air goes, the colder it gets. When air climbing the mountain gets cold, its water vapor condenses and a cloud forms.

story.keeper: That mountaintop always wore a cloud hat. But no clouds form these days, and the flowers up there are wilting…
story.clue: I see a piece on the rock at the top! But it's covered in grey ash.
story.map_clue: A hill by the sea, where a glass cup stands!

kid.intro: This is the cloud and dew lab. The air has water vapor in it that you cannot see.

intro_more.text: When air gets cold, water vapor turns into tiny drops of water. This is called **condensation**. Dew on the grass and clouds in the sky both come from condensation. Let's try it with a cup first.

kid.title: Make a cup cold and make drops form!
kid.say: When air gets cold, its water vapor turns into tiny drops. On a humid day a little cold is enough.

note.law: When air gets cold, its water vapor turns into tiny drops (condensation). So dew forms on a cold cup, and clouds form in air that climbs a mountain.
note.formula: air gets cold → water vapor turns into drops (condensation)
